sentences.show: In 1932, someone climbed a ladder into the nursery of the most famous man in America, and took his baby son.
Charles Lindbergh. The first man to fly solo across the Atlantic.
On 1 March, his little son was gone from his crib. On the windowsill, a ransom note.
$50,000, badly spelled, signed with three holes.
A go-between, John Condon, handed the money to a man in a dark Bronx cemetery. Cemetery John.
The man said the boy was safe. He wasn't.
Ten weeks later, the child was found in the woods, a few miles from home.
Kidnapping across state lines became a federal crime.
But the ransom was a trap. Gold certificates, every serial number written down.
Two years later, a gas station attendant scribbled a licence plate on one of those bills. It led to a German carpenter, Bruno Hauptmann.
In his garage, $20,000 of ransom money. And a wood expert said the ladder matched a board from his attic.
Hauptmann swore he was innocent, refused to confess even to save his life, and died in the electric chair in 1936.
His widow fought to clear his name until she died. Some believe he didn't act alone. Others, that he was framed.
So, the crime of the century, or the frame-up of the century?
The ransom left a trail. Leave one too, and subscribe.
